To shrive means to hear someone's confession of sins, give them a task of penance (something they must do to show true regret), and then formally forgive them — all as an act of religious authority. It is rooted in the Christian practice of sacramental confession, and the word is almost always used in a religious or historical context.

It is an old, literary word. You will not hear it in everyday modern speech, but you will encounter it in older literature, religious writing, and in one very famous cultural expression: Shrove Tuesday.
The Two Sides of the Word

This verb has an interesting quality: it can describe the action from two different points of view, and both are correct uses of the word.

1. When the priest shrives someone:
The priest is the one doing the shriving. He listens to the confession, assigns a penance, and pronounces absolution (forgiveness). In this sense, to shrive is something a priest does to a penitent.

"The old friar shrove the dying soldier before the battle."

2. When a person goes to be shriven:
The ordinary person — the sinner seeking forgiveness — goes to the priest to be shriven. Here, the person is on the receiving end of the act. They confess, they accept penance, they receive forgiveness, and they are now shriven — cleansed of their sins through this formal process.

"She knelt and begged to be shriven before she died."

Both uses are correct and natural, just describing the same event from opposite angles.
The Three Steps That Make Up "Shriving"

To fully understand the word, you need to understand what actually happens during the act of shriving. It is not just one thing — it is a three-part process:

Step 1 — Confession:
The penitent (the person seeking forgiveness) openly admits their sins to the priest. This act of confession is considered essential; you cannot be shriven without honestly declaring what you have done wrong.

Step 2 — Penance:
The priest assigns a penance — a specific act the person must perform to demonstrate genuine sorrow and a desire to make amends. This could be a set of prayers, a charitable act, or some form of self-discipline. It is the outward sign of inner repentance.

Step 3 — Absolution:
The priest formally pronounces that the person's sins are forgiven, speaking in the authority of God (in Catholic and certain other Christian traditions). This is the official release from the burden of those sins.

To shrive someone is to carry out this entire process with them. To be shriven is to have gone through it and emerged forgiven.
Key Verb Forms You Need to Know

Because this word is old, its forms are irregular — and they appear in real-world usage, so you should know them:

  • Shrive — the base form (present tense): "I must shrive you before you go."
  • Shrove — the simple past tense: "The priest shrove him that very evening."
  • Shriven — the past participle (used with "have" or "be"): "He had not been shriven in twenty years."

The past participle shriven is probably the form you will encounter most often in literature and older texts.
Shrove Tuesday — The Word's Most Famous Survival

The clearest trace of this word in modern life is Shrove Tuesday, the day before Ash Wednesday (the beginning of Lent in the Christian calendar). The name literally comes from "shrove" — the past tense of shrive.

On this day, Christians were traditionally expected to go to confession — to be shriven — before the solemn fasting season of Lent began. It was a day of spiritual cleansing and preparation. This is also why Shrove Tuesday is known as Pancake Day in the UK and parts of the world: people would use up rich ingredients (eggs, butter, milk) before the fasting of Lent started. The religious act and the culinary tradition grew up together around the same day.

So whenever you hear "Shrove Tuesday," you are hearing a fossil of the verb to shrive, frozen in time.

Occasionally, writers use "shrive" in a loosely figurative sense — to mean any act of unburdening oneself of guilt, seeking forgiveness, or receiving a kind of emotional absolution, even outside a strictly religious context. For example, a character in a novel might confess a terrible secret to a friend and feel "shriven" afterward — meaning spiritually lighter, as if forgiven. This is a poetic extension of the word's core meaning and works because the emotional experience of confession and forgiveness is universal, even when the religious machinery is not present.

However, this figurative use is not the word's primary meaning. Its heart is always the formal, priestly act of sacramental confession.
Who Uses This Word, and Where?

This is an archaic and literary word. It belongs to:

  • Religious and historical writing about medieval or early modern Christian practice
  • Classic literature — Shakespeare, Chaucer, and other older writers use it naturally
  • Poetry — especially poetry dealing with sin, guilt, death, and redemption
  • Modern writing that wants to invoke a medieval or deeply religious tone

You will not hear it in a normal conversation today. But when you encounter it in a text, you will now know exactly what is happening: someone is confessing, receiving penance, and being forgiven — or a priest is presiding over that sacred exchange.
A Final Summary in One Sentence
To shrive is to formally hear a person's confession of sins, assign them a penance, and grant them absolution — and to be shriven is to have gone through that entire process and emerged forgiven.
